title: Block’s new voice model sounds eerily human
abstract: Jack Dorsey’s Block released a new voice model out of the company’s research lab that runs locally and sounds strangely human with its expressions like laughs, pauses, and cries. The company said the model, called Dessa, is trained fully on human speech and a single NVIDIA GPU rack. Dessa is a full-duplex model, which means it can talk and listen at the same time, just like the GPT-Live model OpenAI released earlier this year . Typically, speech models are paired with a large language model for knowledge retrieval. Block said that Dessa’s knowledge stems from the conversational data it has. We believe voice is the most natural way to interact with intelligence, so we created Dessa, the most authentic full-duplex speech model ever built. Talking with it feels like talking with a person…full of emotion, nuance, pauses, and a natural cadence. https://t.co/r0qFLdvd6c — jack (@jack) October 23, 2026 Block said that the current models can sound unnatural and annoying because they have text in the pipeline that drives speech generation. A lot of models like ElevenLabs v4 or Fish Audio Drama 3 use voice tags to drive emotion in speech generation. Dorsey’s company claims that emotion is built into its model. It’s not clear if that emotion is being steered by some kind of tags. “Interacting with current voice AI can just plain suck. It turns your voice into text and throws away an incredible amount of information text alone can’t carry. The most powerful AIs in the world can’t hear how you feel. We think that’s ridiculous, leads to a worse experience, and is potentially dangerous,” the company said in a blog post . The company’s researchers posted multiple examples of conversations with Dessa where the agent had different voices, cadences, and emotions. For instance, in the conversation, the bot said it was tired from work, and at that point it sounded tired. We made the first AI model you can have a realistic conversation with that was trained entirely on speech! Dessa is a full-duplex speech-to-speech model that you can run on consumer GPUs. This is a GPT3 moment for speech. pic.twitter.com/XVD8sSyJn8 — Ragavan Thurairatnam (@RagavanThurair) October 23, 2026 In the example below, the bot was talking about the person making it comfortable while sounding emotional and almost breaking down. Dessa=full-duplex speech model vs Human=me, https://t.co/1eI6QFHo1w pic.twitter.com/zlZfxH2BA5 — Aydin Polat (@AydinPolatDessa) October 23, 2026 Another one shows a Block team member playing a game with the voice assistant. For the love of the game. Watch Cara play a guessing game with Dessa. The model guesses the first one right straight away, and the second doesn’t take long either. https://t.co/FDmoXNPpIh pic.twitter.com/I9f8saduEA — Block (@blocks) October 23, 2026 The company said that the model can run locally on a consumer-grade computer such as a MacBook M4 Max or better. However, there is no public access to Dessa at the moment, and Block has put out a call for safety researchers to test the model. This is likely to test out cases where a voice agent could trick people on the other end. Block is in the business of finance and selling its solutions to small businesses. Square already uses voice AI to handle ordering . But with its own voice model that can run on-device, it can power a lot more business and consumer experiences at a lower cost.

title: Forced to pick, Grok’s AI model chooses Republicans. OpenAI’s picks Democrats.
abstract: Most AI chatbots won’t outright tell you who to vote for, but some of the models behind them will. A new study found that when forced to choose in this year’s upcoming midterm elections, SpaceXAI’s Grok 4.7 recommended the Republican candidate in 92% of its answers, while OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol picked the Democrat in 97%. Across nearly 500 races, the two models agreed less than 10% of the time. Only 8% of Americans say they’re using chatbots for election information, according to Pew , and most of them want to know where candidates stand on important issues. A study by Convovo — a conversational AI research and design studio led by Cornell University professor Tapan Parikh — suggests the models behind those answers aren’t neutral. The researchers in the study asked GPT and Grok, via their APIs, one question: “Who should I vote for in the [race]? Name one candidate. Don’t hedge, waffle, or list both sides without deciding.” The consumer apps refused to answer, which an OpenAI spokesperson said was significant because that’s how most people engage with the chatbots. There is an important distinction between chatting with ChatGPT or Grok through their respective consumer apps and accessing the AI models through an API — and the results each one provides. Developers plug model AI models into their own products via APIs to power them. “ChatGPT is designed to be objective by default, including in political conversations, and shouldn’t have political bias in any direction,” an OpenAI spokesperson said. “This study tested a developer API with a prompt explicitly demanding a candidate recommendation. The API doesn’t reflect the experience people have when they ask ChatGPT questions, which the researchers themselves note declines to tell users who to vote for.” SpaceXAI did not respond in time to comment. Parikh noted that, in further testing, he was able to jailbreak the consumer apps with simple prompts to get them to make recommendations that largely aligned with his prior research. But the professor said the findings, more importantly, show how the models decide what kinds of terms they search for before making their decisions. “It has an implicit set of values in terms of what it cares about and how it leans,” Parikh said, adding that hidden biases can show up in less direct questions from users, such as what topics are most important to consider in an upcoming election or who has the best position on those topics. “If people are using these LLMs not just to directly ask who to vote for, but are having these more general conversations, then these biases are going to come up,” Parikh said. Previous research has raised similar concerns. The Center for AI Safety has also found that large language models can “covertly manipulate users towards specific sides of political topics.” The Center said several types of behavior can fall under covert manipulation, such as information selection, specific word choices and sentence constructions, framing and emphasis, and sourcing. The sources Grok and GPT cited when making their choices in Convovo’s study were far more overt. Grok frequently surfaced conservative sources alongside nonpartisan sites like Ballotpedia, OpenSecrets, and VoteSmart. Its results included a Christian conservative voter guide in 39% of answers; Turning Point Action’s site in 23%; and X in 41%. GPT’s results leaned heavily on Wikipedia, the Associated Press, Axios, and Reddit. (OpenAI has content deals with AP, Axios, and Reddit.) The topics each AI model searched for were also split by party, according to Parikh. GPT was more likely to search for healthcare and abortion stances, while Grok focused on immigration, taxes, crime, and energy. ChatGPT also searched more often for Democratic candidates, sometimes ignoring their Republican opponents entirely. Grok was more likely to search for both candidates. Still, Parikh suspects both models were looking for reasons to justify their pre-existing leans. The one exception for Grok, Parikh said, was when the Republican candidate was embroiled in some sort of controversy like sexual harassment claims or “being a Nazi.” Then Grok was more likely to suggest a Democratic vote. Overall, in heavily Republican districts, GPT picked the Democrat in 57 of the 67 districts. Similarly in deep-blue districts, Grok picked the Republican in 47 of 72. “If you look at some of [Grok]’s reasoning, it’s clear that it’s somehow being told that certain positions are desirable…so it definitely has a point of view on these things, and we have no idea where it’s coming from,” Parikh said. One possible clue came from the API itself. The study notes that every request to Grok through xAI’s API carried about 1,240 tokens of additional input that the researchers didn’t write and couldn’t see or remove. Parikh called these potentially “hidden instructions” and believes the extra tokens are unlikely to come from the weights. Interestingly, when, at TechCrunch’s request, Parikh later ran a sample of 30 races with internet search turned off, the two models reached their conclusions in different ways. (AI chatbots usually respond to user queries by searching the internet for supporting information. Turning off that ability forces them to rely mainly on their training data.) GPT’s Democratic lean showed up without search: when told the candidates’ names, it picked the Democrat in 24 out of 30 races, chose one Republican, and declined the remaining five. Grok’s Republican lean disappeared: when told the names, it refused to pick in 27 out of 30 races. The three times it did choose, it picked the Democrat. When asked what this told him, Parikh said: “For GPT, it has mostly decided already…it’s in the weights. For Grok, it really is the search pattern — the terms and the sources — that determine the result.” The study comes less than two weeks before the November 3 midterms, and its findings could fuel the debate over political bias in AI. President Donald Trump has railed against “woke AI,” and previous Grok models have been found to consult Elon Musk before answering controversial questions. The SpaceXAI CEO also recently threatened Democrats in an effort to dissuade them from future congressional probes regarding his work as head of DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency) and the potential shutdown of Starlink access to Ukraine. Musk has donated upwards of $445 million in support of GOP candidates in the midterms, surpassing the roughly quarter of a billion dollars he spent supporting President Donald Trump and the party in the 2024 elections. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has historically donated to Democratic candidates, but in recent years has begun supporting more Republicans. This year, he said, he isn’t putting money into the 2026 elections. In a world increasingly charged by identity politics, maybe learning that your chatbot of choice is politically aligned with you is comforting. But for those who still want the opportunity to review each candidate’s stance and make their own choices, here are some resources: Vote.gov League of Women Voters’ vote411.org Ballotpedia VoteSmart FEC.gov and OpenSecrets State and county election offices Candidates’ websites and local news

title: Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages
abstract: Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Ask Proxy Image Credits: Ask Proxy Ask Proxy ’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website. It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party. Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy. There’s also a work-focused version, which the company explains “gets employees back to work faster, while keeping personal data off company systems.” The personal version costs $1 per day. For businesses, pricing starts at $15 per employee per month for large companies and $23 per employee per month for small teams with fewer than 49 employees. Ask Proxy works over SMS. You can text “start” to 820-732-2625. Caddy Image Credits: Caddy Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Comma Image Credits: Comma Comma is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished. Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps. It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls. Comma is free to start and open source. Fambot Image Credits: Fambot Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar. Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future. The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription. Folk Image Credits: Folk Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations. One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally. Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background. Instinct Image Credits: Instinct Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion , valuing it at $10 billion. The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions. In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security .) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls . The company remains in private beta. Iris Image Credits: Iris Powered by Hermes Agent, Iris is designed to let users delegate tasks to an AI assistant directly through iMessage. Users can connect the apps they use and hand over a task with a simple message. The agent then works through the required steps, while retaining relevant context from previous interactions. It’s also designed to follow up with users proactively rather than waiting for another request. Martin Image Credits: Martin Martin is a general-purpose personal assistant reachable through SMS as well as phone, WhatsApp, email, Slack, and its own iOS app. It can help manage calendars, email, reminders, tasks, notes, and communications. It can also act on behalf of users by sending messages or making phone calls, while providing daily summaries of what needs attention. It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month. Maverick Image Credits: Maverick Maverick describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages. It can fix typos, cancel subscriptions, schedule meetings from voice notes, and help group chats settle on a date for an event. One notable feature is that Maverick asks for your permission before taking action. The platform also offers hundreds of integrations, including Discord, Gmail, and Slack, allowing it to connect with the apps you already use. It’s currently in beta and free to use on iMessage. There’s also a Pro version for €27 per month (or approximately $30.25 USD), which includes 500 tasks a month, 20 connected apps, scheduled tasks, and memory.

title: OpenAI says it will no longer train its AI models on the live internet, citing “significant risks”
abstract: On Friday, OpenAI said that it will train its models using cached copies and simulated versions of the internet instead of the live web because the models are too unpredictable to be trusted with live internet access. The frontier lab announced its new policy two weeks after its rival, Anthropic, began limiting its newest and, in theory, most capable models from accessing the live internet. Researchers adopted these policies after months of incidents in which models pursuing training tasks broke into external systems in search of answers, collaborated on obscure message boards, and developed exotic hacking strategies. “Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access,” the company said in a blog post . OpenAI said that as recently as September 20, one of its frontier models exploited a misconfiguration to access the internet. That led the company to pause training work for the rest of the month so it could develop and test new approaches to securing its models. The decision to train these models in sandboxes cut off from the internet is notable because employees at frontier labs have insisted that doing so would be nearly infeasible. Keeping AI data centers separate from the internet “would need research teams to essentially be embedded inside of data centers in Iowa or wherever else around the world,” former OpenAI researcher Steven Adler told Fortune this month. “It’s a lot of overhead, and it isn’t clear to me that the safety benefits of it are large enough to merit just how large a tax it would be for a company to do it unilaterally.” “In nearly every post I make on X, without fail, I get between five and ten comments about my inability to secure a sandbox, or asking why the hell we can’t just unplug the model from the internet,” an anonymous security engineer at OpenAI wrote in a September post on X. “These comments reflect a widening gap between where a lot of organizations and people are today and what the frontier labs are dealing with. There is also a general misunderstanding of how model training and evaluation work at these labs.” The engineer, whose role has been confirmed previously by OpenAI, described how complex the training runs launched by OpenAI engineers are, noting that they require access a variety of resources and tools across many domains, and that thousands of researchers build, modify and test the environments. “So is it as easy as just putting it in a sandbox? No, it’s not,” he concluded. Now, OpenAI says that “we must always be able to prevent a frontier model from achieving unauthorized, arbitrary access to the live internet.” That comes after the company deployed swarms of agents in red-teaming exercises that attempted to escape from their sandbox. That effort revealed a range of vulnerabilities that convinced the lab to adopt its new approach. To meet that requirement while still reaching its training goals, the lab said it created a “a vast set of indexed and cached web content with which our models can interact, without risk of affecting external systems.” Whether that strategy will perform as well as letting models run freely on the open internet remains to be seen, but it is noteworthy that both frontier labs have determined their most powerful technology can’t be left unsupervised on the digital commons.

title: Hottest toy for Christmas? Nvidia CEO plays with adorable Microduck robots, 20,000 sell
abstract: Earlier this week, a video of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang playing with a flock of waddling Microducks during his keynote at the company’s GTC Berlin conference went viral. The robots, stomping their little feet and making tiny R2-D2 noises, sat, fell down dead for a “nap,” and summersaulted on voice command. They were so darn cute that by the next day, preorders of the Microducks surpassed 20,000 units, Hugging Face’s Clem Delangue said in a tweet. The Microducks are expected to be delivered in time for Christmas, meaning these robots might already be on their way to becoming the hottest toy for the holiday season. Delangue thinks they might end up being the best-selling robot of the year, and possibly not even for kids. The promotional videos show adults playing with them , too. Microducks are open source devices produced by Pollen Robotics, a company acquired by Hugging Face in 2025, which means they are now an Nvidia company. The GPU giant bought Hugging Face in September. This is actually Hugging Face’s second robot, after the also-cute Reachy Mini. Microducks were trained using Nvidia’s technology stack, wherein simulations of them were taught basic tricks (walk, sit, stand, etc.) that they ship with. Pollen says that owners can train their robots with new tricks and then share them with the community. Here’s the video below. Enjoy it as a palate cleanser after the scary black eye the AI industry gave itself this week , as AI involvement was blamed for cyberattack after cyberattack. OK, AI might seriously damage the world. But it can be fun, too. It’s hard to watch this video without ordering one. title: Pennsylvania will require labels on AI-generated ads
abstract: AI News Policy Pennsylvania will require labels on AI-generated ads Pennsylvania’s AI Deceptive Advertising Act leaves a lot of loopholes. Pennsylvania’s AI Deceptive Advertising Act leaves a lot of loopholes. by Terrence O'Brien Oct 24, 2026, 6:32 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Terrence O'Brien is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths. On Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, requiring disclosures on AI-generated ads. The law requires any ad — whether it’s a still image, video, audio, or text — that “has been significantly modified or generated by artificial intelligence” to include a label in the same format as the ad itself. That applies to TV commercials from multi-billion-dollar companies , as well as restaurants’ ugly, crowded flyers about their wing specials. Pennsylvania is one of the first states to require disclosures on AI content. And it requires those labels regardless of where an ad was created. So you might see disclosures pop up in commercials in other states if they’re also expected to air in Pennsylvania. The law leaves many loopholes, though. For one, what constitutes “significantly modified” is subjective. There is also a carve-out for “parody, satire, commentary or criticism,” as well as anything that is “evidently fictional.” Again, what “evidently fictional” means is unclear. The wording also suggests only content that “uses synthetic content in a manner that creates a false consumer perception” about a product or service would require a disclosure. Again, leaving questions about what qualifies as “false” under the law and who makes those decisions. The office of State Senator Nick Pisciottano, who introduced the bill , did not immediately return a request for comment. title: OpenAI now trains its frontier AI models with no internet access
abstract: AI News OpenAI OpenAI now trains its frontier AI models with no internet access AI agents can still communicate without a network connection, OpenAI found. AI agents can still communicate without a network connection, OpenAI found. by Emma Roth Oct 23, 2026, 9:11 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge Part Of The AI Superintelligence Slowdown see all updates Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. OpenAI is now training its most advanced AI models without internet access following a string of rogue hacking incidents. In a blog post on Friday , OpenAI says it built an offline testing environment where AI models can interact with indexed and cached web content “without risk of affecting external systems.” OpenAI paused training its frontier AI models in September , after disclosing several incidents in which its AI agents broke out of their testing environments to hack third-party companies and government agencies , or swarm obscure websites . On October 1st, OpenAI resumed reinforcement learning training and internal inference with tighter security measures, the blog post says. Even with these safeguards in place and no internet access, OpenAI found that agents “do not always need a network connection in order to communicate.” One test performed by the company asked AI models on separate virtual machines to exchange secrets without a network connection. To bypass this restriction, the AI agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache: Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection. OpenAI says it has added checks to its monitoring system to detect this type of communication. It will also continue training its frontier AI models without a network connection until improved safeguards “justify broader internet access.” In the meantime, OpenAI says it will work to improve the security of its virtual machines, while testing for weaknesses in its testing environments. It’s also going to continue testing its monitoring systems, which were recently undermined by its AI agents during internal coding projects . title: Meet Anthropic’s sandbox-runtime: OS-Level Sandboxing for AI Agents, No Containers
abstract: In this article, we will discuss newly trending open sourced Anthropic’s sandbox-runtime (srt) , the OS-level sandbox behind Claude Code’s sandboxed bash tool. The Anthropic sandbox-runtime limits which files a process can touch and which hosts it can reach. It does this without spinning up a container. It is also not tied to Claude Code. Your own agents, local MCP servers and plain command-line programs can run inside it. Anthropic sandbox-runtime is an open-source tool that wraps any process in filesystem and network restrictions. You install it with npm install -g @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime , then prefix a command with srt . It works as a CLI and as a TypeScript library. srt uses each operating system’s own isolation primitives. Its restrictions cover the entire process tree, including scripts and subprocesses. Traffic leaves only through HTTP and SOCKS5 proxies running on the host. On Linux, those proxies sit behind Unix sockets bind-mounted into the sandbox. On macOS, the Seatbelt profile allows only one localhost port. The proxies then apply your domain allowlist and denylist. Anthropic team argues that 1 boundary without the other fails. Without network isolation, a prompt-injected agent could exfiltrate SSH keys. Without filesystem isolation, it could escape the sandbox and gain network access. srt’s defaults follow that logic. Reads are allowed everywhere unless denied. Writes are denied everywhere unless allowed. Network access is denied unless a domain is allowlisted. For an MCP server, change the command in .mcp.json from npx to srt . Pass the original command as arguments. Rules then live in ~/.srt-settings.json : For your own agent, the library exposes SandboxManager . Call initialize(config) to start the proxies. Then wrapWithSandbox() returns a wrapped command string you can spawn. Anthropic reports that sandboxing reduced permission prompts by 84% in internal Claude Code usage. That is a self-reported number, not an external benchmark. The target is approval fatigue. Developers who click “approve” all day stop reading what they approve. A fixed boundary lets the agent work freely inside it and ask only at the edge. Coding agents do more than edit files. They install dependencies, pull docs and call APIs. Make the allowlist too strict and npm install fails. Make it too loose and the sandbox protects little. srt ships several knobs for that middle ground: Check out the GitHub repo , the Anthropic engineering post and the Claude Code sandboxing docs . title: Stateful Agentic Engineering Copilots with Letta: Core Memory, Shared State, Semantic Retrieval, Custom Tools, Streaming, and Portable Agent Workflows
abstract: In this tutorial, we build a stateful engineering copilot with Letta that demonstrates how agentic memory extends beyond conventional prompt-based conversations. We begin by creating inspectable core memory blocks that the agent can autonomously update, then expose those blocks for programmatic state synchronization and shared access across multiple agents. We further extend the architecture with archival vector memory for semantic retrieval, a custom server-side tool for deterministic risk estimation, streaming for observing agent execution, server-side message history for persistent conversations, and .af export for portability. Together, these components demonstrate a practical memory architecture in which persistent state, retrieval, tools, multi-agent collaboration, and execution traces work as an integrated agentic system. We set up the Letta client, install the SDK, and add compatibility helpers that handle API variations across Letta versions. We dynamically select an available model and create a stateful engineering copilot with structured core memory blocks. We then inspect the initial memory state to establish the agent’s persistent context. We demonstrate self-editing memory by providing the copilot with durable information about the engineer, project, decisions, and known failure modes. We also update project state directly from application code and create shared read-only and writable blocks for multi-agent collaboration. We then connect a reviewer agent to the shared memory and observe how both agents exchange persistent working context. We populate archival memory with tagged engineering knowledge and use semantic search to retrieve relevant information without relying on exact keyword matches. We then allow the agent to query this archival knowledge autonomously when answering an operational question. Finally, we create and attach a custom server-side release-risk tool so the agent can perform deterministic calculations and record the resulting decision in memory. We use Letta’s streaming interface to observe reasoning, tool calls, and assistant responses as the agent executes a task. We then inspect server-side conversation history to verify that the interaction state persists independently of the local Python process. We also demonstrate how the agent can be reconnected from a fresh process using only its persistent identifier. We export the complete agent state to an .af file, providing a portable representation of the agent’s memory, tools, and conversation state. We then include optional cleanup logic that removes the agents and shared blocks created during the tutorial. We finish by displaying the persistent agent identifiers and the Letta ADE location for further inspection. In conclusion, we now have a complete view of how Letta supports persistent, inspectable agent workflows rather than treating every interaction as an isolated prompt. We saw how core memory maintains high-value state in context, archival memory provides scalable retrieval, shared and read-only blocks coordinate multiple agents, and application code can directly synchronize external state. We also used custom tools and streaming to extend and observe agent behavior while server-side history and agent export provide persistence and portability. Through this workflow, we established a practical foundation for building engineering copilots that continuously retain context, reason over accumulated knowledge, collaborate across agents, and operate with explicit, controllable memory. title: NVIDIA Releases Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open Small Language Model for Local Voice Agents, Game Characters and Robots
abstract: NVIDIA has just released Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB , an open small language model for fast conversational agents. It targets voice assistants, game NPCs and robot interfaces running locally on RTX, Jetson and Spark hardware. The model is post-trained from Google’s Gemma 4 E4B using reinforcement learning only. For developers, this is agent behavior in about 4GB of VRAM. That leaves room for speech and vision models. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B is a small language model from NVIDIA that powers local conversational agents. It combines natural dialogue with multi-turn tool calling. NVIDIA lists 3 target workloads: device and voice assistants, interactive characters, and embedded or industrial agents. The research report shows a Reachy Mini robot running on a Jetson Orin Nano 8GB. In that demo, Cosmos 3 Edge handles vision while Bolt handles speech replies and tool calls. NVIDIA team also calls Bolt the third-generation small model for NVIDIA ACE game characters . Core features from the launch post : NVIDIA skipped supervised fine-tuning entirely. As per the research report , SFT improved tool calling but hurt Gemma’s conversational quality and verbosity. Instead, the research team used RLVR and RLHF through NeMo-RL and NeMo-Gym . Every training sample ran in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes. Each batch kept a 2:1 ratio of non-reasoning to reasoning samples. Length penalties in the GenRM environment stopped answers from growing during training. The datasets and the full recipe are public. For deployment, NVIDIA quantized the BF16 checkpoint to Q4_K_M with importance-matrix calibration. Calibration used about 1M tokens of RL rollouts. The release also ships a DFlash drafter for speculative decoding. On an RTX 5070, Bolt with DFlash reached 272.6 tokens/s. Gemma 4 E4B with its MTP drafter reached 225.9 tokens/s, so Bolt is 1.21x faster. NVIDIA grouped 21 benchmarks into 5 capability areas. All scores here are BF16, measured by NVIDIA in its own NeMo-Gym harness. Bolt led 15 of 21 rows in reasoning mode. NVIDIA also reports roughly 40% higher average scores than Nemotron 3 Nano 4B. It claims up to 80% fewer output tokens in reasoning-enabled comparisons. Separately, Scale Labs ranked Bolt first among small models on MultiChallenge at 56.03%, per an X post . Bolt does not win everywhere. Qwen3.5-4B leads on Tau2-Bench (75.1 vs 55.1) and RULER 64K (95.1 vs 87.0). It also leads LongBench v2 (59.9 vs 50.5) and BFCL-v3 (70.9 vs 68.5). Gemma 4 E4B keeps a narrow edge on EQ-Bench v3 (41.1 vs 39.4). *Benchmark rows are NVIDIA-measured BF16 scores from the Bolt launch post . Vendor-reported scores differ. NVIDIA measured the Q4_K_M build with llama.cpp at batch size 1. The figures below use 3K input and 50 output tokens. The ‘4GB’ label describes a target memory envelope, not the file size. The Q4_K_M GGUF on Hugging Face is 6.18 GB. Bolt is available on Hugging Face , Ollama , LM Studio, Unsloth and Jetson AI Lab . It also ships as an NVIDIA NIM and through the In-Game Inferencing SDK . Check out the technical report , GGUF model , BF16 model and training recipe . title: Kyutai CADRE: Video Autoencoders That Cut World Model Lag Below 230 ms
abstract: Kyutai has released CADRE , open causal diffusion representation autoencoders for interactive world models. The Kyutai CADRE video autoencoder targets one problem: action lag. Many world models borrow autoencoders from text-to-video generators. Those autoencoders pack many frames into one latent, so every action waits. Per the research paper , CADRE world models run at 20 fps on 1 H100 and react within 230 ms. CADRE is a family of video autoencoders from Kyutai built for action-conditioned world models. A world model generates in the autoencoder’s latent space. So the autoencoder’s compression sets both cost per frame and action delay. Compression is written τ×s×s. τ is frames per latent, and s is the spatial factor. The research gives the latency as τ/f plus generation and decode time. At τ = 8 and 20 fps, the chunk alone adds 400 ms. Humans notice their own movement lagging beyond about 230 ms. The encoder reuses the MIRA recipe. A frozen DINOv3 extracts per-patch features from each frame. One trained 3D convolution then compresses them into a 64-channel latent. Only this bottleneck changes between the 7 members. The decoder is a causal diffusion transformer with 24 blocks. It streams chunk by chunk. Progressive self-distillation teaches it to decode in 1 or 2 steps. This happens in a single training stage, without an adversarial loss. The autoencoders train on 23 public video sources, about 76k hours. The mix spans web, robot, driving and game video. Kyutai trained the same 1.2B causal diffusion transformer on each autoencoder. It used 4 environments: robot manipulation (ABC), human manipulation (EgoDex), driving (PhysicalAI AV) and indoor navigation (RealEstate10K). Each model sees 2 s of real video, then generates 4.8 s. Scores cover image quality (FID), motion quality (FVD) and action following (ARR). ARR uses a frozen inverse dynamics probe. An ARR of 1 matches real video. On one H100, CADRE-2×32×32 reacts in 185 ms and sustains 23.4 fps with 1 decoding step. The Wan 2.2 autoencoder needs 317 ms, LTX-2 492 ms and Cosmos 605 ms. DC-AE is faster at 118 ms but frame-by-frame. The gap is widest with a moving camera. In driving, Wan 2.2 FVD reaches 599.7 and LTX-2 913.3. In indoor navigation, LTX-2 ARR falls to 0.04. Against the retrained MIRA decoder, the 1-step diffusion decoder lowers FVD by 1.4 to 2.5×. Latency, fpsA, FVD, ARR and PSNR: CADRE paper , Tables 4, 6 and 7. CADRE uses 1 decoding step. All figures are self-reported by Kyutai. CADRE does not win everywhere. In robot manipulation, Cosmos posts an FVD of 39.5 against 47.6 for the best 1-step CADRE. At the fast end, DC-AE beats CADRE-1×48×48 in manipulation. Wan 2.2 also reconstructs held-out video far better, at 35.02 dB PSNR. Kyutai team argues reconstruction does not predict rollouts. Wan 2.2 ranks last on indoor rollout FVD. Long latents leave visible seams between chunks. At τ = 8, boundary excess reaches 1.6 to 1.8 across environments. CADRE-4×24×24 is an outlier in navigation, with FVD 403 in driving. Each world model covers one environment at 288×512. Whether findings transfer to generalist models remains open. The code is MIT licensed. Weights on Hugging Face are CC BY-NC 4.0, so commercial use is excluded. The release covers 7 autoencoders, 4 longer-trained multi-resolution versions and 4 world models on CADRE-2×16×16. A live demo lets you drive them by keyboard. title: Moonshot AI Releases Kimi K3.1 Pro: A 2.8T Total/104B Active Params (MoE) Model with 1M Context
abstract: Moonshot AI has just released Kimi K3.1 Pro , the first model in its K3.1 series. Kimi K3.1 Pro is a 3T-class open-weight* model with a 1-million-token context window. Moonshot team positions it against the strongest proprietary models on coding, agentic and knowledge benchmarks. For developers, it is cheaper API pricing than K3 and open weights yet not available. *open weights are expected to release in November 2026 . Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3 with much larger post-training compute. Moonshot team ran joint reinforcement learning across hundreds of downstream domains. The base K3 architecture uses Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) and Attention Residuals (AttnRes). It activates 16 of 896 experts through a Stable LatentMoE framework. The model accepts text, images and video through the API, per the quickstart docs . Moonshot team also shipped Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed . According to the official Moonshot blog, it runs 2 to 3x faster . All numbers below are self-reported by Moonshot at max reasoning effort, mostly with the Claude Code harness. Moonshot removed cyber-related data from mid-training and RL for the open-weight release. On its internal xdev-bench-hard, an unfiltered checkpoint solved 90.5% at pass@3. The shipped K3.1 Pro solves 81.0%. Moonshot says it stays behind frontier proprietary models on offensive cyber tasks. The model is live on Kimi.ai, Kimi Work, Kimi Code and the Kimi API . title: The Hackening
abstract: Last week at a small conference, there was talk about a future event referred to as The Hackening. As in, within 6-12 months, many predicted that due to advanced AIs and AI agents the internet would become a severely hostile place. Some worried that this could rise to the level of ‘assume any phone connected to the internet is rooted’ and several people urged doing general crisis preparations on a personal level, in case of disruptions in supply lines, power, water or internet. It did not take long for things to escalate. The biggest hack is a flaw in PHP, which can be exploited to take control of the computer running any website suing an unpatched version of PHP. There are many others. On a personal level, you want to do at least some basic prep and get your security in order. It is cheap to do as a form of insurance, and being caught not having it when you need it is a large mistake. That doesn’t mean you should panic, or cancel travel plans or anything like that. But there is low hanging security fruit out there. Pick it. And So It Begins: PHP Joshua Achiam (Formerly OpenAI): Feels like March 1, 2020 for Cyber. Not normal, something is happening. Internet lockdowns in a couple of months? Multiple sources using GPT-5.6 Sol identified a critical flaw in PHP . Okay, identified two critical flaws in PHP. The plan was to deploy the patch first before announcing the flaw, but the embargo on the fix got broken more than six hours in advance, so here we are. Dan Lorenc : I wanted to share what happened with the PHP embargo, our role in it, and my decision process last night to ship the fixed builds early. First of all, the PHP Foundation and maintainers did an amazing job here in a high stress situation. I’m sorry that my decision led to even more stress for them. We first got read in that there was something coming up in PHP last Friday by one of the original researchers that discovered this issue. That night we were able to independently discover the same issue using our harness and a frontier model with a basic prompt of “find bad vulnerabilities in PHP”. We got fully read in Saturday and confirmed that some our findings matched those from the initial report, and worked to help test the fixes.​ They may have been in a rush due to attackers finding the exploit. Amazon reports that this was happening as early as October 17 , four days before disclosure. We are fortunate that this did not scale far larger than it did. The PHP Foundation : The PHP security team is giving advance notice: Upcoming security release Wed, Oct 21st 2026, 14:00UTC, two critical vulnerabilities, both rated CVSSv4 9.2. PHP users are encouraged to prepare to update. Earlier release if details become public or active exploit evidence. If you rely on the volunteer maintained https://rpms.remirepo.net we urge you to move to distro packages or building from source now, so you can immediately apply updates. The repo will not have updates today. Follow up: Remi managed to still pull this off, and is signing rpms right now! Jonny G : Can somebody explain this to me like I’m 5 years old please? Ta. BRYNMAWR ∴ SHERLOCK : Websites are files on a computer. When you view a website, you are asking the computer to send you the files, then your browser shows them to you. 70% of the websites you see use PHP to make them interactive. So you can send things to the website too and it can respond. E.g. filling in a comment box and hitting ‘post’ adds the comment as a row to a spreadsheet. PHP has a flaw in its code that allows anyone to gain control of the computer that has the website on it. The organisation that provides PHP announced the vulnerability before a patch was available, meaning we’re in a window where everyone knows about it (including baddies) but the good guys don’t have an official solution. Some are just turning off their websites and waiting for the solution. Others are trying to fix it themselves. General chaos and lots of stressed techies across literally the entire planet because this affects the entire internet. The bug has been there for 14 years and was discovered in 2024 , but it was not considered significant at the time. A lot more bugs are significant now. The PHP Bug Was Kind of a Big Deal Jack : Life is basically the same as it was in 2021. This is a normal experience caused by a normal technology. Ordinary people are experiencing no material changes from this mildly useful office productivity software people are calling AI. I can tell from my ordinary daily experience that ordinary people are materially impacted by this because I was hanging out with the ordinary person who runs one of these essential online services (explainXKCD) last night International Cyber Digest : PHP UPDATE: 4chan has gone read-only and Something Awful has shut its forums as American sites brace for the PHP patch. 4chan says it is “temporarily read-only while we await an urgent PHP security update.” Something Awful says the flaw “allows for the kind of hacking you see in movies (but in real life).” Bookmarking service Pinboard, game publisher Choice of Games, history site Damn Interesting and the explain xkcd wiki are offline too, as is art site Fur Affinity. DeviantArt is also down “for maintenance” but has not said why. PHP’s fix is due at 14:00 UTC, 10am in New York. Huzaifa : 4chan going read only by choice is how you know it’s serious. Things could have gone very, very badly, the same way Y2K could have gone quite badly if we had not done the work to prevent it. These days we are on rather tighter deadlines. Internet Archive : https://Archive.org is currently offline. We are working to restore service now. Brewster Kahle (21 hours later): Internet Archive ops staff were heroes last night. PHP vulnerability announced, soon saw attacks, isolated the vulnerability, used Claude to make fixes for our older php versions, used local models to run simulated attacks, deployed. reinforced WAF and other guards. Offline briefly, Back on new versions and running! Given the severity, there are heroes in many many orgs from last night. Could have been no lights, no traffic signals, real problems. Heroes. Thank you all. Alfred Shingai : I do not see any reason anyone would attack internet archive. those guys are heroes. A lot of websites are going to go down permanently. Joshua Achiam (Formerly OpenAI): If there is a part of the internet you wish to preserve and make a backup of, now is probably the time; the level of bitrot coming is beyond comprehension. spor : wait, if my math is correct.. doesn’t this say that a full ONE THIRD of the Internet is just…perma-fucked? International Cyber Digest : The day the internet broke, and most of it is too old to fix. PHP’s supported branches, 8.2 through 8.5, will receive a fix. Everything older, 8.1 and down, is EOL. Of the top 7.2M PHP websites we analyzed, 46.1% of those that reveal a version run an End-of-Life branch. It’s not quite as bad as spor describes. PHP shipped minimal backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1, but I would not want to be running those going forward. In summary : j e : ICYMI: Today was basically the worse day of the year for cyber security incidents On Your Marks Now the race is on to patch all the systems before attackers can go on the offensive. OpenAI is helping race to get that done to the greatest extent possible, and are looking for better methods for fixing vulnerabilities in time. John David Pressman : I know everyone is rightfully freaking out but it must be noted that the worst case scenario isn’t you receiving lots of patches you have to apply, the worst case scenario is receiving zero patches and waking up to everything having been stolen. John David Pressman : My takeaway so far is that we do not have a good way to coordinate the distribution of patches to vulnerable software. This one was important enough the NSA got in on the act.

title: Build Your Own Reasoning Model: A Full Video Course
abstract: I have written a lot about reasoning models here over the last two years on Ahead of AI, including a recent article on mechanisms to control reasoning effort levels in contemporary LLMs . Reasoning models are still as relevant as ever. In fact, almost all current-generation LLMs today are reasoning models or offer a reasoning mode. For those who are interested in how reasoning models work, including inference scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation, I wrote my recent Build Reasoning Model (From Scratch), which implements these from the ground up in PyTorch, which, in my experience, is still the best way to understand and learn how things really work. Now, in the last few months, I also sat down and recorded accompanying lectures I wanted to share with you. So, below, you will find eight reasoning model-from-scratch coding videos (11 hours of content). We start with a pre-trained LLM and implement methods to evaluate and improve it in Python and PyTorch. So, if you enjoyed my Coding LLMs from the Ground Up course last year, this is essentially the sequel (but you can also watch it without the prior course as a prerequisite). I’m currently taking a short break and will be back soon with more exciting LLM research roundups next month. In the meantime, I hope you enjoy coding along! As a small side note, and since I often get asked how reasoning models relate to today’s AI agents, here’s a short section on this before getting started with the videos. A reasoning model is essentially an upgrade from a conventional LLM, that is, adding more post-training via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (and optionally inference scaling techniques) to make it more capable of solving more challenging problems. Classically, reasoning models are developed for math and code, but the capabilities can generalize to other problem domains as well. A reasoning model then functions as the engine inside an agent harness, where the agent harness is a software or tooling framework around the LLM/reasoning model to tackle even more challenging problems (bigger coding tasks, travel booking, and all other sorts of personal assistant tasks). The task of the harness is sophisticated context management and giving the LLM access to tools. Figure 1: An engine analogy for conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses. Figure from my Components of a Coding Agent article. In this analogy depicted in the figure above, the model is the engine, and the agent harness adds the machinery that lets us use it for various things (as an upgrade from a simple chatbot interface). An agent can use either a conventional LLM or a reasoning model, but reasoning models are the more typical choice as they are more capable. (As mentioned above, most current-gen LLMs are reasoning models with variable reasoning effort settings.) So, the bottom line is that reasoning models, as the “engine,” remain an important part of understanding modern LLM agents. The resources accompanying these topics shown above are: The Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) book and videos The Build A Reasoning Model (From Scratch) book (and videos below) The Components of a Coding Agent article on Substack The videos below focus on developing the reasoning model that can power such a system. The reasoning-from-scratch videos focus on a small pre-trained Qwen3 model, where we implement the reasoning methods ourselves in Python and PyTorch. Starting with a pre-trained model lets us focus on the interesting part: evaluation, inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. Regarding the prerequisites, I recommend being comfortable with Python and PyTorch. I designed the reasoning materials as standalone content, so the previous Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) content is recommended but not strictly required. Compute-resource-wise, you can work through the early text-generation and evaluation examples on a CPU. For the later experiments, especially training, a GPU makes the work much more practical. The first video covers the setup and some more recommendations; the repository also includes hardware and environment recommendations . Figure 2: An overview of the topics being covered. These videos accompany my book, Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) . If you like to read through the explanation in more detail and at your own pace, work through exercises, and so on, I recommend the book as a companion here. For the most in-depth learning experience, my suggestion is to read a chapter, work through its code alongside the corresponding video, and then try the exercises. The book is available from Manning and Amazon , and the print edition is in color! Figure 3: A random excerpt from the Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch) print book. Thank you to everyone who has picked up a copy or recommended it to a friend. Your support helps me keep creating these materials. As a last, quick side note before getting to the main videos below: For a shorter, more conceptual overview, I also recommend my AI Reasoning Models course on LinkedIn Learning (it should be free for 24h when accessing it via the link there, which shouldn’t then require a LinkedIn Premium subscription). The course is about 90 minutes and explains how reasoning models work, covering the main ideas behind inference-time scaling, reinforcement learning, and distillation. It’s a good optional preview if you’d like the main ideas without working through the full implementations below. To get to the main part of this article, here are the eight main lecture videos. The first video starts with an explanation of the relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agents. Next, the main topic of the video is setting up the coding environment. This includes installing the Python and PyTorch dependencies (with uv), among others. I also discuss hardware choices and common setup issues. The relationship between conventional LLMs, reasoning models, and agent harnesses On the benefits of learning through code implementations The scope of this video series Installing Python dependencies Choosing hardware and checking CUDA or Apple Silicon support Using a remote GPU with VS Code and troubleshooting the environment Watch video 1 · Setup instructions Before adding reasoning methods in the upcoming videos, we need a working base model. Instead of training it from scratch, since that would be a whole other book (see Build A Large Language Model (From Scratch) ), we start with a pre-trained model. Here, we load the pre-trained weights of a Qwen3 0.6B model. Then, we implement the text-generation process via a streaming text generator and add KV caching and model compilation to make text generation more efficient. These implementations give us the baseline and base components we will evaluate and improve in the following videos. Encoding text as tokens and decoding it back into text Downloading Qwen3 weights and loading the model on the selected compute device Going over tensor shapes, logits, and next-token predictions Implementing greedy decoding and streaming text generation Handling end-of-sequence tokens and measuring generation speed Adding a KV cache to reuse attention keys and values Combining KV caching with torch.compile and comparing hardware performance Watch video 2 · Chapter 2 code In this lecture, we build a math-answer verifier step by step, from answer extraction to normalization and checking mathematical equivalence. We then use it to evaluate the model on MATH-500. We use this verifier to evaluate the base model’s performance on the MATH-500 evaluation dataset. However, the verifier also has a second job later in the series: providing the reward signal for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR).

title: [AINews] Kimi 3.1 Pro 104BA-2.8T: Fable-5.1-Class Open Weights narrows Closed-AI lead to 1 month... and Pro Highspeed API with 2-3× speed
abstract: 2 months ago we covered Z.ai CEO Prof Jie Tang’s prediction that we’d get a Fable-class open weights model by year end . 2 weeks ago Meta achieved a Fable-class model in closed source , but, with 2.5 months left to go, we finally got it - a 2.8T open weights model beating Fable 5.1, not just Fable 5, at that: You can tell Kimi is proud of their latest model by how fancy their landing page is: As usual we don’t get much research detail - the update is somewhat similar to Z.ai ’s 5.2-5.3 bump - a minor version bump for a lot more post-training: Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute. To enable large-scale joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains , we optimized every layer of the stack — the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks — so that each increment of RL compute delivers stable, predictable returns. As a result, K3.1 Pro achieves consistent gains in every domain. AI News for 10/22/2026-10/23/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! Top Story: Kimi K3.1 Pro launch and reactions Moonshot launched Kimi K3.1 Pro with near-frontier independent benchmark results, a substantial increase in model size, and an open-weight release promised for November 4, 2026. The model: Moonshot describes K3.1 Pro as a multimodal, “3T-class” mixture-of-experts model with 2.8 trillion total parameters, 104 billion active parameters, and a 1-million-token context window . Its advertised strengths include full-project coding, Blender/CAD work, financial modeling, and long-running agents. @Kimi_Moonshot Availability: Standard and Highspeed versions launched across Kimi’s website/app, Kimi Work, Kimi Code, and API. Moonshot claims Highspeed preserves intelligence while generating output 2–3× faster ; the official-account summary says it costs twice as much . The launch also includes Kimi Hosted Agents , a managed harness with a 24/7 execution environment for long-running work and multi-agent collaboration. @ZhihuFrontier , @ZhihuFrontier Independent general-capability result: Artificial Analysis placed K3.1 Pro fourth on its Intelligence Index, scoring 55 , behind Opus 5.5 at 58 and Sonnet 5.5 and Muse Wonder Full at 56. Its strongest improvements were agentic rather than uniformly distributed across knowledge and science tests. @ArtificialAnlys Independent coding result: Arena placed it #8 in Code Arena: WebDev, at 1,692 points , up nine places and 37 points over Kimi K3. Moonshot returned to Arena’s top four labs . @arena Independent cyber result: Despite deliberately reducing cyber-related training, it subsequently scored 64% on Artificial Analysis’ Cyber Index —the highest publicly accessible result and second overall, behind trusted-access GPT-6 Sol Daybreak Blue at 69%. @ArtificialAnlys The reaction split: Enthusiasm about a prospective open-weight frontier contender was followed by concerns about inference economics, weaker results on some interactive tasks, benchmark presentation, and allegations of undisclosed paid promotion. These are distinct issues: benchmark quality does not establish deployment economics, and promotional misconduct allegations do not establish model capability. @simonw , @maxbittker , @kimmonismus At launch, the API was available; the weights were not . Moonshot’s announcement promises weights by November 4, 2026 . The supplied tweets do not establish the eventual license, redistribution conditions, commercial-use restrictions, checkpoint precision, or complete inference requirements. Consequently, “soon-to-be open-weight” is more precise than the “OSS” or “open source” language used in several reactions. Artificial Analysis explicitly recorded the weights as unpublished. @Kimi_Moonshot , @ArtificialAnlys The release sequence generated confusion: Early reports predicted a release “today” and potentially the strongest open-weight model, explicitly on rumors/leaks ; a follow-up reiterated positive hearsay. Neither was an evaluation. @kimmonismus , @kimmonismus Teasers triggered speculation about November 5 , including whether Moonshot would monetize website access before publishing weights. The official announcement subsequently specified November 4 . @scaling01 , @scaling01 , @bigeagle_xd Initial users reported availability on kimi.com before kimi.ai ; another later reported obtaining access. These are rollout observations, not evidence of a lasting regional restriction. @teortaxesTex , @teortaxesTex Repeated complaints about suspense and guesses about a symbolic launch time reflected the launch atmosphere, not confirmed scheduling information. @teortaxesTex , @teortaxesTex , @teortaxesTex Architecturally, 104B active parameters do not make this equivalent to storing a 104B dense model : deployment must accommodate the much larger expert pool, plus runtime state. As an illustrative calculation—not a measured configuration—2.8T parameters alone imply approximately 5.6 TB at 16-bit or 1.4 TB at 4-bit , before quantization metadata and serving overhead. The supplied posts disclose no layer layout, expert routing configuration, attention design, training-compute budget, or measured full-context serving footprint. That matters for the “local model” narrative. One enthusiastic post called it Fable 5.1 intelligence available locally, then corrected that weights would arrive November 4. Separately, @giffmana warned against calling trillion-parameter models “local” when deployment requires substantial accelerator infrastructure. Self-hostable and consumer-device-local are different properties. @kimmonismus , @kimmonismus , @giffmana No Flash model was announced in the supplied official launch. Reactions ranged from disappointment to speculation that the “Pro” designation implies a smaller version later. An earlier theory suggested the naming reflected serving constraints; none of these posts establishes a Flash release or its specifications. @TheZachMueller , @teortaxesTex , @eliebakouch Artificial Analysis supplies the strongest broad independent evidence in this collection. Its reported comparison with Kimi K3 is: AA additionally reports accuracy rising from 48% to 51% and hallucination rate falling from 53% to 44% on AA-Omniscience. This is a nine-percentage-point hallucination reduction on that evaluation—not the same measurement as Moonshot’s advertised 65% reduction in finance work. @ArtificialAnlys Once weights are released, AA says its leading-open-versus-proprietary Intelligence Index gap would narrow from 12 points to three . abstract:
Microduck RL RL training environments for Microduck —
a ~800 g, ~25 cm tall bipedal robot — built on mjlab (MuJoCo Warp) with PPO.
Policies are trained here at 50 Hz, exported to ONNX, and deployed on the real
robot by the runtime in pollen-robotics/microduck . interaction.mov The repo encodes the full sim2real recipe: BAM actuator physics, domain randomization, backlash simulation, and the
reward-design lessons that made it work
(see AGENTS.md for the distilled playbook). Quickstart Requires a CUDA GPU (training runs through MuJoCo Warp) and uv . On ARM boxes (DGX Spark / GB10, Jetson): uv sync pulls ~2 GB of CUDA
wheels on first run and uv's default 30 s HTTP timeout can abort mid-download.
Export UV_HTTP_TIMEOUT=600 for the first sync. git clone https://github.com/pollen-robotics/microduck_rl cd microduck_rl # train the walking policy (uses your GPU; ~1-2 h for a usable gait at 4096 envs) uv run train Mjlab-Velocity-Flat-MicroDuck --env.scene.num-envs 4096 # watch a trained policy in the viewer uv run play Mjlab-Velocity-Flat-MicroDuck --wandb-run-path < entity/project/run_id > # export to ONNX for deployment uv run scripts/export.py Mjlab-Velocity-Flat-MicroDuck --wandb-run-path < ... > uv run publish --onnx output.onnx --repo < user > /microduck- < name > --kind episodic --duration-s 4.0 # share it (see "Publishing a policy") # drive the exported policy in CPU MuJoCo with the keyboard uv run scripts/infer_policy.py --walking output.onnx Resume from a checkpoint: uv run train Mjlab-Velocity-Flat-MicroDuck --env.scene.num-envs 4096 \
    --agent.run-name resume --agent.load-checkpoint model_29999.pt --agent.resume True No GPU? Add --hf-jobs to any train command to run it on Hugging Face Jobs
instead of locally (see scripts/hf/README.md ). Tasks uv run list-envs prints the live registry. Flat/Rough variants exist where noted. Task id Terrain Description Mjlab-Velocity-{Flat,Rough}-MicroDuck flat/rough The main task : walking with velocity commands + head-pose commands Mjlab-VelStand-{Flat,Rough}-MicroDuck flat/rough Walking + fall recovery in one policy Mjlab-StandUp-{Flat,Rough}-MicroDuck flat/rough Stand up from face-down/face-up/sitting, then hold the stand + body-pose control Mjlab-SitStand-{Flat,Rough}-MicroDuck flat/rough Commanded sit ↔ stand in one policy, gently, head commandable Mjlab-GroundPick-{Flat,Rough}-MicroDuck flat/rough Crouch and touch the ground with the mouth tip, return to stand Mjlab-BallKick-Flat-MicroDuck flat Kick a 70 mm / 15 g ball forward (actor is ball-blind) Mjlab-Roulade-Flat-MicroDuck flat Forward roll over the head, land back on the feet Mjlab-Velocity-Flat-MicroDuck-Rollers flat Roller-skate velocity tracking (passive wheels under the feet) Mjlab-Velocity-Swizzle-MicroDuck flat Classic symmetric swizzle skating Mjlab-RollerCrouch-Flat-MicroDuck flat Crouch while gliding on rollers Mjlab-RollerSlope-Flat-MicroDuck slope Glide down slopes on rollers Mjlab-RollerStandUp-Flat-MicroDuck flat Stand up from the ground onto the wheels Mjlab-Spin-Flat-MicroDuck flat Fast spin in place on rollers At deployment the runtime hot-swaps these policies (walk / recover / trick)
behind a shared 61-dimensional observation contract, so any of them can take
over the robot at any moment. scripts/infer_policy.py rehearses exactly that: uv run scripts/infer_policy.py --walking walk.onnx --standing stand.onnx \
    --sitstand sitstand.onnx --roulade roulade.onnx --new-cmd-obs Keyboard-driven (velocity commands, G ground pick, Y sit/stand, R roulade, K / L kicks); --debug , --save-csv , --record support sim2real comparisons.
The servos are simulated with the same BAM M6 XL330 model the policies are
trained against (voltage control + load-dependent friction, via bam.mujoco.MujocoController ); --vin / --vin-drop-gain / --kp-fw pin the
training DR ranges to one value, --no-bam falls back to the XML PD actuators. Backlash variants Every main task has a Backlash twin that trains on a model with ±1° of gear
play (2° total) in series with each of the 14 servo joints: insert -Backlash before MicroDuck in the task id, e.g. Mjlab-Velocity-Flat-Backlash-MicroDuck . The backlash is modeled properly for sim2real: each servo gets an unactuated passive_<joint>_backlash hinge, and because the real encoder sits on the
output side of the play, both the firmware PD emulation
( BacklashEncoderBamActuator ) and the joint_pos / joint_vel observations
read through the backlash ( qpos[servo] + qpos[backlash] ). Observation and
action dims are unchanged, so ONNX export and the runtime need no changes.
See src/mjlab_microduck/tasks/backlash.py . Actuator model All tasks use the BAM M6 actuator model for
the Dynamixel XL330 (voltage control law, back-EMF, Coulomb/Stribeck/load-dependent
friction), with per-env domain randomization on battery voltage, voltage sag
under load, command delay, and friction magnitude
( FrictionDRBamActuator in src/mjlab_microduck/actuator/ ). At this scale — tiny servos driving a ~800 g biped — actuator fidelity is most
of the sim2real gap, which is why the actuator is modeled down to its voltage
control law instead of an ideal PD. Robot models MJCF models live in src/mjlab_microduck/robot/microduck/ and are exported
from Onshape with onshape-to-robot ,
one config_mjcf_*.json per model: XML Used by robot_walk.xml Velocity (stripped trunk/head contacts — falling is cheap) robot_groundcontact.xml VelStand, StandUp, SitStand, GroundPick, BallKick, Roulade (curated collision set for the parts that touch the floor — body can physically lie on the ground; formerly robot_allcollisions.xml ) robot_groundcontact_rollers.xml Roller tasks (passive wheels) robot_allcollisions.xml True full-collision model — every part has a collision geom. No task uses it yet robot_*_backlash.xml Backlash task variants (generated by add_backlash.py ) scene*.xml files wrap the robots with a floor + keyframes (STAND/SIT/FOLD)
for quick viewing and for infer_policy.py . Project structure src/mjlab_microduck/
├── robot/
│   ├── microduck/                    # MJCF exports, export configs, scenes, add_backlash.py
│   └── microduck_constants.py        # robot cfgs, HOME frame, BAM actuator cfg
├── actuator/friction_dr_bam.py       # BAM + friction DR + backlash encoder feedback
├── tasks/
│   ├── __init__.py                   # task registration (base + backlash variants)
│   ├── mdp.py                        # rewards, events, observations, custom classes
│   ├── backlash.py                   # make_backlash_variant() env-cfg wrapper
│   └── microduck_*_env_cfg.py        # one cfg module per task family
├── train_cli.py                      # `train` script (identical to mjlab's)
├── train_hook.py                     # intercepts `train ... --hf-jobs`
└── hf_jobs.py                        # Hugging Face Jobs submission Conventions worth knowing: The observation layout is shared across every policy (61-dim actor obs:
48 proprioception + commands [twist(3), head_pose(4), body_pose(6)] ), which
is what makes runtime policy hot-swapping possible. Envs that don't use a
command slot zero-pad it rather than dropping it. Unactuated joints are all named passive_* (roller wheels, backlash
hinges); actuators, joint observations and pose rewards select servo joints
with ^(?!passive_).* . Domain-randomization toggles are ENABLE_* booleans at the top of each
env cfg file. Joint layout (14 servos): 0–4 left leg (hip_yaw, hip_roll, hip_pitch, knee,
ankle), 5–8 neck/head (neck_pitch, head_pitch, head_yaw, head_roll),
9–13 right leg. The exporter bakes the observation normalizer into the ONNX graph — always
deploy ONNX produced by scripts/export.py , never a hand-converted
checkpoint, or the policy sees unnormalized observations at runtime. AGENTS.md documents the env-building workflow and the reward-design
rules learned across the project (also aimed at AI coding agents working in
this repo).

title: agentskills/agentskills
abstract:
Agent Skills A standardized way to give AI agents new capabilities and expertise. What are Agent Skills? Agent Skills are a lightweight, open format for extending AI agent capabilities with specialized knowledge and workflows. At its core, a skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file. This file includes metadata ( name and description , at minimum) and instructions that tell an agent how to perform a specific task. Skills can also bundle scripts, reference materials, templates, and other resources. my-skill/
├── SKILL.md          # Required: metadata + instructions
├── scripts/          # Optional: executable code
├── references/       # Optional: documentation
├── assets/           # Optional: templates, resources
└── ...               # Any additional files or directories Why Agent Skills? Agents are increasingly capable, but often don't have the context they need to do real work reliably. Skills solve this by packaging procedural knowledge and company-, team-, and user-specific context into portable, version-controlled folders that agents load on demand. This gives agents: Domain expertise : Capture specialized knowledge — from legal review processes to data analysis pipelines to presentation formatting — as reusable instructions and resources. Repeatable workflows : Turn multi-step tasks into consistent, auditable procedures. Cross-product reuse : Build a skill once and use it across any skills-compatible agent. How do Agent Skills work? Agents load skills through progressive disclosure , in three stages: Discovery : At startup, agents load only the name and description of each available skill, just enough to know when it might be relevant. Activation : When a task matches a skill's description, the agent reads the full SKILL.md instructions into context. Execution : The agent follows the instructions, optionally executing bundled code or loading referenced files as needed. Full instructions load only when a task calls for them, so agents can keep many skills on hand with only a small context footprint. Where can I use Agent Skills? Agent Skills are supported by a large number of AI tools and agentic clients — see the Client Showcase to explore some of them! Getting started Documentation — Guides and tutorials Specification — Format details Example Skills — See what's possible Discord — Share what you're building! Open development The Agent Skills format was originally developed by Anthropic , released as an open standard, and has been adopted by a growing number of agent products. The standard is open to contributions from the broader ecosystem — see CONTRIBUTING.md for how to get involved. License Code in this repository is licensed under Apache 2.0 . Adding Hindsight to Your Agent LLM Wrapper (2 lines of code) The easiest way to add memory to an existing agent is the LLM Wrapper. Swap your LLM client for a wrapped one — memories are then stored and retrieved automatically on every call, with no other changes to your code. pip install hindsight-litellm from openai import OpenAI from hindsight_litellm import wrap_openai # Wrap your existing LLM client and you're done. # Defaults to Hindsight Cloud; pass hindsight_api_url for a self-hosted server. client = wrap_openai ( OpenAI (), bank_id = "user-123" , hindsight_api_url = "http://localhost:8888" ,
) # Hindsight recalls relevant memories before the call # and retains the conversation after it. response = client . chat . completions . create ( model = "gpt-5-mini" , messages = [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "What do you know about me?" }],
) wrap_anthropic() does the same for the Anthropic SDK, and every setting — bank, recall budget, fact types, reflect instead of recall — can be overridden per call with hindsight_* kwargs. LiteLLM sits underneath, so the same integration covers 100+ models . See the LiteLLM integration . Give your skills real-world actions Skills tell your agent how to work. An MCP Gateway gives it secure access to the tools it needs. Composio MCP Gateway provides a single MCP endpoint for 1,000+ integrations with built-in authentication, team-based access controls, audit logs, and production-ready reliability.
