title: Node2Shell evolves to HTTP2Shell, blast radius affects many HTTP libs and apps
abstract:
Node2Shell evolves to HTTP2Shell. Brotli flaw (CVE-2026-111497) blast radius affects many libraries & apps using HTTPs. Buckle up. Written by Dania Durnas Published on: Oct 23, 2026 Last updated on: Oct 24, 2026 TL;DR ⚠️ Brotli is a widely used compression library from Google. On Wednesday, October 21st NodeJS disclosed CVE-2026-111497, dubbed “node2shell,” wherein a Node.js process that decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data can be made to leak memory or run arbitrary code. On Thursday, Python disclosed that Python packages were vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497 as well. On Friday, October 23rd, it has become known that this CVE affects other major languages and service applications using HTTP, where patches are not yet fully available. Check if you are decoding Brotli as a dependency within your libraries. Stay on guard for wider announcements and be ready to upgrade as soon as possible. If there is no patch available for a library or application that may be affected, we recommend disabling Brotli decoding until patches become available. Update 4:12PM PT: Patches are available for libbrotli , Python , C++ , NodeJS , bun , Envoy and more coming. Apache and Nginx do not decode brotli by default. Update 4:15 PM PT: OpenAI shares that they discovered this vulnerability in February. While the root cause issue was fixed in the Brotli source code at the time, it wasn’t known that it gave rise to a security vulnerability. OpenAI's advisories here . ‍ What is Brotli? Brotli is a lossless compression algorithm and data format developed by Google. It’s a way to make data smaller for storage or sending over the internet. Software then unpacks it to recover the original data. It’s widely used for HTTP compression to compress web content such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. What is CVE-2026-111497? CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write in the Google Brotli decoder affecting versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms. This is the same Brotli decoder flaw behind Node2Shell announced a couple days ago. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted Brotli-compressed stream to corrupt memory, leak sensitive data, crash the process, or potentially execute arbitrary code. It carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 (Critical), and Node.js is affected through its bundled Brotli library. A bug makes the Brotli decoder keep accepting more bytes when it should reject the data. Those bytes can overflow a small working buffer and damage the program’s memory. An attacker can use that damage to control what runs, such as their own code. OpenAI found this in February reported it as unauthenticated remote code execution that works in both directions, so a malicious client can take over an unpatched server and a malicious server can take over an unpatched client that accepts compressed responses. The root cause was fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn't recognized as a security issue at the time and no release shipped with the fix until now. That means every project that bundles Brotli has to ship its own update. ‍ You’re exposed if any environment has Brotli 1.2.0 or earlier or brotlicffi 1.2.0.x installed, since HTTP clients such as requests, httpx, and aiohttp load these packages automatically when they’re present. Upgrade to Brotli 1.2.1 or brotlicffi 1.2.1.0 and rebuild any container images that bundle them. As of October 23, advisory databases don’t map the CVE to either PyPI package, so pip-audit, Dependabot, and Safety won’t flag vulnerable versions yet. ‍ You can see what we’ve tracked here in Aikido Intel. Python C++ Libbrotil NodeJS As for unaffected software, Apache’s standard mod_brotli does not decode Brotli How to patch HTTP2Shell CVE-2026-111497 For CVE-2026-111497, update the affected runtime or Brotli library: Node.js: upgrade to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1 , or a newer supported release in the corresponding release line. Native Brotli / libbrotli: upgrade to 1.2.1 or later . For older release lines, use patched 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 . Python packages: upgrade Brotli to 1.2.1 or later and brotlicffi to 1.2.1.0 or later , wherever installed. curl / libcurl: update its Brotli dependency to 1.2.1 , a patched older release, or the vendor’s security-fixed package. Bundled or statically linked copies require an updated application build. Bun: upgrade to 1.4.4 or later . Rebuild compiled executables that bundle Bun. Envoy: upgrade to 1.40.0, 1.39.3, 1.38.6, or 1.37.8 , or a newer release in a supported branch. 1.36.12 also includes the fix, but the 1.36 branch is unsupported. Istio: the fix is included in 1.29.9, 1.30.6, and 1.31.2 . Use a newer supported release in the corresponding line; the 1.29 branch is end of life. Operating-system packages: install the vendor’s security update. Vendors may backport the fix without changing the upstream version number. Other HTTP servers, reverse proxies, API gateways, and HTTP clients: update the affected runtime or Brotli library they use. Where Brotli is bundled into the product, install the product vendor’s release that explicitly addresses this CVE. For managed services, confirm remediation with the provider. Update dependency locks, rebuild affected applications and container images, redeploy, and restart services. Verify that running workloads use the patched components. ‍ Fixed releases, reviewed October 23, 2026 Project Patch status Fixed versions Notes Node.js Patch available 22.23.4 · 24.22.1 · 26.12.1 Use a supported release line. Bun Patch available 1.4.4 Includes Brotli 1.2.1. Envoy Patch available 1.40.0 · 1.39.3 · 1.38.6 · 1.37.8 1.36.12 also includes the fix, but 1.36 is unsupported. Use a supported branch. Istio Patch available 1.29.9 · 1.30.6 · 1.31.2 1.29 is end of life, so move to a supported line. Google Brotli (upstream) Patch available 1.0.10 · 1.1.1 · 1.2.1 Choose the fixed release for your library branch. What to do if you can't upgrade yet These workarounds reduce exposure while you prepare the upgrade: Python applications: where Brotli support is optional, uninstall both Brotli and brotlicffi from affected environments. Remove dependency extras such as httpx[brotli] and any other requirements that would reinstall them, then regenerate dependency locks and rebuild/restart workloads. HTTPX, Requests, and urllib3 retain gzip and deflate support without these optional packages. However, a server that sends Brotli anyway may produce an unreadable response or an application error; automatic fallback is not guaranteed. Uninstalling both Python packages and restarting workloads removes the decoding paths provided by those packages for incoming and outgoing data. It does not remove separate Brotli decoders bundled into other runtimes, libraries, or products. Incoming HTTP requests: reject requests whose Content-Encoding includes br at the reverse proxy, load balancer, or application middleware, before any vulnerable decoder processes the body. Match br case-insensitively, including within lists of encodings. Outbound HTTP requests: remove br from Accept-Encoding. Also disable Brotli response decoding or reject responses whose Content-Encoding includes br before decoding begins. Ensure this check occurs before automatic body processing; checking after the client has downloaded and decoded the response is too late. Changing Accept-Encoding alone is insufficient: a malicious server can send a Brotli response regardless of what the client advertises, and urllib3 selects its decoder from the response’s Content-Encoding header. Keep these controls in place until affected components are patched and verified. Review coverage as vendors confirm additional affected components or attack paths. How Aikido helps with CVE-2026-111497 Aikido flags vulnerable versions of Brotli and brotlicffi in your repositories, container images , and dependencies, including when they arrive as transitive dependencies.

title: Sony Retires Its Last 4K Blu-ray Player in Japan, PS5 Is All That's Left
abstract:
Friday, October 23rd 2026 Sony Retires Its Last 4K Blu-ray Player in Japan, PS5 Is All That's Left by DrUsmanSaleem Yesterday, 12:36 Discuss (19 Comments) Sony has stopped shipping the UBP-X700/K in Japan, its last standalone 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray player in the country. Shipments ended on October 22, and according to Sony retailer Kunkoku , the remaining stock on Sony's Japanese store sold out almost immediately. There's no word on a successor. That leaves the disc-equipped PlayStation 5 as the only Sony product in Japan that can still play 4K Blu-ray movies. The UBP-X700/K only launched on May 17, 2025, as a cut-down version of the 2018 UBP-X700 without streaming apps, and it was last listed at ¥58,300. Sony will keep selling the BDP-S1700/K, though that one only handles regular Blu-ray discs. The PS5 is not a perfect stand-in for home theater enthusiasts either. title: Neural chip decodes interactions between brain regions

Neural chip decodes interactions between brain regions Import & publish the news × Are you sure you want to import this news into ? This news will be sent to its subscribers. Yes No LogSync chips, measuring approximately 4x2 mm. 2026 EPFL / Lundi13 - CC-BY-SA 4.0 EPFL researchers have developed an implantable neural chip that tracks communication across brain regions, identifying cognitive and emotional states in real time. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a therapeutic technique that delivers electrical pulses to specific areas of the brain via an implant to modulate neural activity. It is already widely used for movement disorders such as Parkinson’s disease, and researchers are increasingly exploring its potential for severe psychiatric illnesses including major depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder. However, most existing DBS systems operate in what engineers call an “open loop” manner: stimulation is delivered according to predefined settings rather than continuously adapting to the patient’s brain activity. Even among closed-loop, or adaptive systems, many rely on signals recorded from a single brain region. This is a major limitation for psychiatric disorders, where clinically relevant information may be distributed across networks of interacting brain regions. “Our work is based on the growing body of research suggesting that psychiatric disorders arise more from disruptions in communication between brain regions than from dysfunction of any single region,” explains Mahsa Shoaran, head of the Integrated Neurotechnologies Lab in EPFL’s School of Engineering and Neuro-X Institute. The INL team at EPFL's Geneva campus. From left: Amitabh Yadav, Jieun Joo, Mahsa Shoaran, Jinhan Liu, and Daney Alex. 2026 EPFL / Lundi13 - CC-BY-SA 4.0 Shoaran and her team have developed a low-power, implantable neural system-on-chip. Dubbed LogSync, it records brain activity and extracts biomarkers that describe the strength of brain waves (oscillations) and synchrony between signals from different brain regions. A machine-learning algorithm then analyzes these network-level biomarkers to distinguish cognitive and emotional states, and generate stimulation triggers when specific states are detected. The work, published in the IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits , was developed as part of a CHF 6.6 million grant from the US National Institute for Mental health (NIMH) to develop implantable systems capable of measuring and controlling oscillatory brain networks for severe psychiatric illnesses, particularly mood and anxiety disorders. It builds on the lab's previous work on brain-to-text decoding and closed-loop neuromodulation , extending these concepts to network-level biomarkers and adaptive decoding for future psychiatric therapies. More targeted stimulation at lower power The researchers evaluated LogSync using human brain recordings from previous psychiatric experiments. One dataset captured changes in cognitive engagement while performing a mental task, while another captured emotional arousal as participants viewed video clips. The algorithm distinguished these cognitive and emotional states from the neural recordings alone. In further experiments conducted in rats at the University of Minnesota, the implant tracked ongoing oscillations and generated stimulation triggers at predefined phases of brain activity. The LogSync chip, measuring approximately 4x2 mm. 2026 EPFL / Lundi13 CC-BY-SA 4.0 Shoaran says that major challenge was achieving all this functionality while working within the very limited power budget of an implantable system. “Our entire system is co-designed, meaning the algorithms and hardware are developed together with the constraints of implant in mind. This approach helped us achieve network-level neural signal processing and decoding on a single chip, while keeping power consumption under 200 microwatts — a fraction of that typically required by many implantable neural-interface systems,” she says. Another innovation is LogSync’s use of logarithmic computations, which simplify the complex operations needed for brain-network analysis and real-time biomarker extraction and decoding. LogSync's initial validation focused on psychiatric applications. But the capability to extract brain-network biomarkers to trigger precisely timed stimulation is broadly applicable across next-generation neurotechnology, including adaptive DBS for movement disorders, closed-loop non-invasive stimulation, and emerging focused-ultrasound interfaces. In parallel, the laboratory is developing new machine-learning methods that learn directly from neural recordings rather than predefined biomarkers. Their recent ICML 2026 work, which uses self-supervised learning to capture neural activity across regions, channels, and time, supports broader efforts to bring intelligent neural interfaces closer to clinical applications, including through Infera Neuro , an EPFL spin-off co-founded by Shoaran. title: UUIDv7: Timestamps aren’t time-ordered and other oddities
abstract:
Built on Shards of Silicon This post is part of a collection on UUIDs . I’m going to call it. UUIDv7 is weird. Most blog posts about UUIDv7 tout these benefits: monotonically increasing IDs a helpful timestamp of when the object was created; and unguessable IDs But none of these properties are strictly held.
Certain RFC compliant implementations of UUIDv7 violate these properties to extreme degrees.
The only useful property UUIDv7 appears to strictly provide is uniqueness and therefore collision resistance.
I’ve already discussed how UUIDv7 IDs can be guessable ,
so this post explores the other properties. Is the timestamp useful? Superficially, it seems that embedding a timestamp in the ID can remove the need to track the creation time in a separate database column, providing marginally more efficient database operations.
If you need to list things ordered by creation time very often, it’s useful if the primary index gives that behavior, removing the need for another index. Unfortunately, the timestamp embedded in a UUIDv7 ID may not relate to the object creation time.
The Postgres docs for uuid_extract_timestamp helpfully warn that “the extracted timestamp is not necessarily exactly equal to the time the UUID was generated”. RFC 9562 allows implementations to alter the timestamp field, using values that aren’t strictly derived from the system clock.
This relates to the tension between UUID monotonicity and timestamp accuracy.
In certain scenarios, the difference between the timestamp and the current time can be arbitrarily large. Implementations MAY alter the actual timestamp. — RFC 9562 §6.1 This specification makes no requirement or guarantee about how close the clock value needs to be to the actual time. — RFC 9562 §6.1 … implementations MAY increment the timestamp ahead of the actual time … — RFC 9562 §6.2 Incrementing the timestamp ahead of the system clock is an interesting problem.
If the generator is seeing so much load that a counter field is regularly overflowing then the timestamp could accelerate into the future.
Using a sufficiently large counter would be wise and the RFC says the minimum size SHOULD be 12 bits.
A counter overflow would require a pretty aggressive creation rate, over 4,096 IDs per millisecond per node, which is beyond the limits of many systems.
This overflow becomes relevant, however, if the timestamp freezes; which I’ll discuss in a later section. Example: Python uuid.uuid7() One prominent implementation that increments the timestamp is the Python standard library’s UUIDv7.
The increment happens only in certain circumstances, like when the counter overflows.
Unfortunately, the generator can get stuck in an increment cycle if the clock ever jumps backwards and the timestamp can race ahead of the system time by an arbitrarily large amount. Here’s a simple example: import uuid
from datetime import datetime # Prime the generator with the current time
t = uuid.uuid7().time
now = datetime.now()
delta = (datetime.fromtimestamp(t/1000) - now).total_seconds()
print("Initial delta: ", delta)
# Ask the user to change the time
input("Set clock back one hour") while True: for _ in range(100000): uuid.uuid7() t = uuid.uuid7().time now = datetime.now() delta = (datetime.fromtimestamp(t/1000) - now).total_seconds() print("New delta: ", delta) Which gives: $ uv run --python 3.14 main.py
Initial delta: -0.000748
Set clock back one hour
New delta: 3695.277581
New delta: 3795.042411
New delta: 3894.80756
New delta: 3994.573106
^C We expect the difference to be 3600 seconds (one hour) as the implementation refuses to allow the embedded timestamp to jump backwards and we expect the difference to decrease as the system clock catches up to the frozen timestamp.
But when the load is above one ID per millisecond the difference will increase without bound.
At lower loads it will take longer for the system clock to catch the timestamp, but we don’t see the runaway effect. The related issue shows Python developers reasoning that this is consistent with the RFC, is consistent with other implementations, and that there isn’t “much we can do” on a “flawed system”.
I think these points are correct as I see this same behavior in other implementations.
Nevertheless, it would be helpful if existing UUIDv7 implementations could handle system clock jumps without runaway behavior.
There are many real-world examples of clocks jumping backwards, even decades out of sync in time-sensitive environments. Is leaking a timestamp harmful? Embedding the timestamp in the ID means that you cannot share the ID without also sharing the timestamp. It’s pretty difficult to think of an example where this really matters.
One example could be a user profile page that doesn’t disclose when the account was created, but the UUIDv7 ID in the URL leaks the high-precision timestamp. This issue would typically be very low on my list of security concerns because I find much more severe problems when I do security assessments.
Nevertheless, there are contexts where this matters and engineering resources would be focused on addressing it.
If you’re in the latter camp, be wary of UUIDv7 leaking metadata. Are UUIDv7s monotonic? This section is even more pedantic, so skip ahead if you’ve had enough.
Briefly: UUIDv7 IDs provide some sort of rough order, which may be suitable for your requirements. When I was reading the UUIDv7 RFC I was surprised to see it describing a method for creating IDs across different nodes that are monotonically ordered.
This was proven impossible back in the 1970s ,
and lead to the development of vector clocks and similar technology. At a high level, the problem is that system clocks cannot be synchronized to a suitable precision.
Ordering things by timestamp only works if you know precisely what time it is.
Any uncertainty in the time results in uncertainty of event ordering. Succinctly: Timestamps are only time-ordered if you know what time it is and you don’t know what time it is. For this reason, similar ID formats claim to be nearly sorted.
It seems odd that UUIDv7 makes a stricter claim and does not deliver on them.
At the very least, the challenges of synchronizing clocks across systems make the millisecond and especially the sub-millisecond timestamps quite suspect. But even on a single node, using a single implementation, UUIDv7 IDs are not strictly monotonic.
The easiest way to get out-of-order UUIDv7 IDs is to use an implementation that uses a millisecond timestamp without a counter.
This approach trivially generates out-of-order IDs inside a small for loop . So no, there’s nothing in the UUIDv7 specification that would ensure the IDs are strictly monotonically increasing.
Specific implementations may do better than others (with sub-millisecond timestamps, counters, well-synchronized clocks, etc), but we’ve known since the 1970s that this problem is not strictly solvable. In UUIDv7’s favor, roughly ordered IDs are still quite useful.
So don’t rip UUIDv7 out of your systems just yet.
Just be wary of what assumptions you have. Restarting a UUIDv7 generator The RFC has lots of discussion about the handling of clocks that jump backwards.
Timestamps are only time-ordered if clocks tick forwards, so special care is needed. We’ve already discussed one mitigation: tracking the last generated timestamp to ensure that an earlier timestamp is never used.
To do this safely you’ll need to write the last used timestamp to persistent storage, such that you can read it again after a system reboot or a process restart. I’ve looked at several UUIDv7 implementations I couldn’t find one that writes timestamps to persistent storage.
So implementers seems disinterested in addressing the issue and they generate out-of-order IDs when a process restart follows a clock jumping backwards. Looking at real-world clock synchronization problems, you’ll find many examples of clocks getting set to future dates .
